To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the neurodynamics of a simulated neural network that is a function of the scotomas derived directly from the retinal image of a patient can accurately predict their visual performance, that our approach is more sensitive to the effects of the disease on the visual system than traditional clinical metrics, and that this approach can be used to evaluate the efficacy of treatments at the level of expected changes in high level visual perception.
we have developed a computational framework for predicting the perceptual consequences (i.e. psychometric performance) of AMD by decoding neurodynamics simulated from an individual's retinal image.

we are able, for the first time, to accurately predict individual subject psychometric performance using simulated neurodynamics and that we are able map the disease on the individual's retina to a representation (simulated neurodynamics) that is a substantially stronger predictor of psychometric performance than traditional clinical measures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a computational framework for understanding how the state of a patient's retina is translated into the perceptual consequences for that individual.
the development of computational models of early visual processing that can be applied to the characterization of visual function in individuals with age-related macular disease.
developing a framework for characterizing the perceptual consequences associated with retinal pathology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we have shown that a computational neurodynamics model of early visual cortex can accurately predict the visual performance of patients with AMD, and that the model can be used to map the retinal disease onto a representation of visual function that is substantially better than traditional clinical metrics.

our approach identifies possible new metrics to evaluate the efficacy of treatments at the level of expected changes in high level visual perception and typifies how computational models can be used to characterize perceptual consequences of retinal pathologies.

we have shown a new way of characterizing the perceptual consequences and progression of AMD, and we have identified new metrics that may prove useful in the development and evaluation of treatments for this debilitating disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a computational framework that can be used to map early visual disease to high-level perceptual dysfunction and that this framework can be used to predict perceptual changes in individuals with early visual disease.

the perceptual consequences for AMD can be quantitatively predicted by a computational model that incorporates the state of the individual retina, and that this is a better predictor than traditional clinical metrics.
the perceptual consequences for AMD are not just a function of the size of the scotoma, but also the shape and distribution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
computational models of early visual processing can be used to predict the consequences of early visual diseases.
the computational neural model can be used to map retinal abnormalities to high-level perceptual deficits in a subject specific way.
computational models can be used to predict the perceptual consequences that result from a specific disease pathology.
